pages.text:
*Garden Log, Day 105: Practicing: speaking. Results: none.*

The Community Hall smelled of damp carpet and instant coffee. Three hundred chairs faced a white screen where a pie chart rotated slowly. Ms. Vandermeer stood at the front in a grey suit that fit so well it looked like a second skin. Her hair was pinned up with a clip that caught the light.

"We are proposing a comprehensive redevelopment," she said, her voice crisp and bright. "Parking for two hundred vehicles. Green spaces. A much-needed tidying of the estate's periphery."

A woman in the front row nodded vigorously. A man in a beanie checked his phone. The pie chart turned. It showed the garden as a small, grey sliver labeled *LAND*. It was not grey because it was empty. It was grey because it did not matter.

I gripped the plastic arms of my chair until my knuckles turned white. The plastic creaked. It was a small sound, but in the silence between Ms. Vandermeer’s sentences, it sounded like a crack in a glass plate.
pages.image: A large community hall with rows of plastic chairs facing a projector screen showing a grey pie chart; a woman in a neat grey suit stands at a podium, while a girl with round glasses grips the chair arms tightly in the foreground.

pages.text:
I had a plan written in purple ink on the back of my hand, the letters slightly smeared from the humidity. It said: *Say the garden exists. Ask them to look.*

I had practiced this in the mirror of our flat, and I had even said it to Yusuf, who had looked bored, and to the bean in the yogurt cup, which had not responded, as usual. I felt ready, which is a word I use too often, but tonight it felt true.

Ms. Vandermeer clicked to the next slide. It was a render of cars, silver and identical and gleaming.

"Does anyone have questions?" she asked.

My hand went up. It rose above the heads of the people next to me, thin and brown and trembling just once. Every head in the room turned toward me, and I counted three hundred faces, then realized that counting was not the point.

My mouth opened. The words were there, waiting in the purple ink on my skin.
pages.image: A close up of a thin, brown-skinned hand raised high in a crowded room, with the blurred faces of an audience turning to look; the background is out of focus but suggests a bright, sterile meeting space.

pages.text:
"I... it... never mind."

The words came out dry and flat, like a biscuit that had fallen off the counter and been picked up from the carpet. I lowered my hand. I sat down. The plastic chair squeaked under my weight, a sound that seemed to hang in the air long after I had stopped moving.

A man in the row behind me coughed. It was a polite cough, the kind that says *I heard that, but I am choosing to ignore it*.

Ms. Vandermeer turned to me. Her smile did not waver. It was professional, warm, and utterly empty.

"Perhaps after the meeting, dear," she said.

It was the worst thing anyone had ever said to me. Not because she was unkind, but because she believed me. She believed that I was a child who had been confused. She did not see the garden. She did not see the rules. She saw a grey sliver on a chart.

Theo sat next to me. He did not look at me. He did not leave. He just watched the screen, where the silver cars were still gleaming, and said nothing.
pages.image: A girl with round glasses and a green pencil in her hair sits slumped in a plastic chair, looking down at her hands, while a boy in a beanie sits beside her, both facing a blurred audience and a bright stage.

pages.text:
At the back of the room, near the fire exit, Mr. Osei stood holding his cap in both hands. He turned it over and over, the brim rubbing against his palms until the wool looked worn. In the dim light of the hall, he was very tall and still, looking like a shadow that had forgotten how to move.

His eyes were fixed on the screen. The grey sliver of *LAND* was still there, bright against the dark. I watched his face closely. It was not angry, and it was not sad, but it was the face of a man watching a boat leave a harbor that he had spent thirty years repairing.

He did not raise his hand. He did not speak. He just stood there, his keys jingling softly against his belt, a sound like a distant, quiet bell.

The meeting ended with polite applause. The lights came up, harsh and white, and the grey sliver vanished into the darkness of the projector.
pages.image: A tall, thin man with a grey moustache stands at the back of a dim room, holding a cap in his hands, his face turned toward a bright, blurry projection screen, while the rest of the room fades into shadow.

pages.text:
The air outside was cool and carried the sharp, damp smell of wet concrete, which settled in my nose as I sat on the steps, legs dangling over the edge. I watched the streetlights flicker on, one by one, like a row of tired eyes opening slowly after a long nap.

Mrs. Ilves came down the steps in her slippers, the soft *thwap-thwap* of them against the pavement keeping a quiet, rhythmic beat. She was eighty-something, knitted to the chin in a thick wool shawl, and she looked at me with eyes that seemed to see right through my skin and into the messy room behind it.

"It's easier to bloom in the dark than under a lamp," she said.

I shook my head. "I don't know what that means."

"I don't either," she said, sitting down beside me with a heavy sigh that rustled her knitting. "But it sounded good." She patted my knee, her hand dry and warm against my denim jacket. "I have known you for one hundred and five days, Sana. And I think you are very brave."

I looked at the dark fence at the end of the road, where the pavement ended and the rail cutting began. "I froze," I said.

"Yes," Mrs. Ilves said, pulling a strand of yarn through her fingers. "Then you'll thaw."
pages.image: An elderly woman in slippers and a knitted scarf sits on concrete steps next to a girl with a denim jacket, both looking out at a dark, wet street with flickering lights, the mood quiet and contemplative.
